title: Going to Chicago when Jelly was sick; his new car
summary: He wrote he was sick, she came for three weeks and stayed a year; he borrowed a car and told her he was 28.

story.theme_name: Chicago: the jazz migration and its clubs
story.community_name: Going north: working the Chicago jazz scene

blocks.x: Mm-hmm. Uh, had—you say he was sick in Chicago?
He was sick in Chicago. And it happened something like Walvash Street, Walvash Avenue, Walvash. He lived on Walvash and I lived on Everhart.
Did he stand for you or did you just hear he was— No.
Did he ask you to come up? No, he was just writing and telling me he was sick and I just came up.

And I came up for three weeks and I stayed a year. Stayed a whole year. Mm-hmm. Was he sick all that time? No, he was playing music and writing music and having— Well, I mean, whenever he'd tell me not to come in, it's because he was having company. Yeah. And he said he wanted to study or something like that. But I was stopping on Everhart Street where he lived on Walvash. Right. I can't remember where now though. Mm-hmm. It's been such a long time.

And people up there tell me he lived around 35th Street along there or something. Like I said, the start of the music center where all the clubs were. Yeah. And the music stores and publishers. Is that so?
Well, I don't remember going to any place with him but going up to—
Oh, you said something about when he met you. Did he—did he meet you at the station and he borrowed a car or something? He had a mama in an old car.

He's old. And he met me and the next day he came out in a new car and got me. He said, now this is my automobile. Now remember, sister, I'm now but 28 years old. I don't know how old you are. And he knew he was so much older. But men don't want children, not more than women. I said, 28, Jolly. And he didn't give me a chance to say any more than that. But he'd come and take me out every day after he got better. And I stayed over at Miss Martin's on Everhart Street.
